scenes.name: Benny Goodman, el rey del swing
scenes.author: Ted Gioia
scenes.desc: La Depresión hunde la venta de discos y el fin de la ley seca desmitifica el jazz, pero la radio en cadena crea el estrellato: managers como Hammond, Glaser o Mills median entre arte y masas. Goodman, hijo de inmigrantes judíos de Maxwell Street y clarinetista de técnica clásica, prepara su triunfo en el programa Let's Dance de la NBC (con arreglos de Fletcher Henderson, «King Porter Stomp», «Sometimes I'm Happy») y estalla en el Palomar Ballroom el 21 de agosto de 1935: nace la era del swing y el fenómeno de fans que anuncia a Sinatra, Elvis o los Beatles. Con Hammond rompe la barrera racial en sus combos (Teddy Wilson, Lionel Hampton, Charlie Christian), lleva el jazz al Carnegie Hall en 1938 y encarga obras a Bartók, Copland y Hindemith. Gene Krupa populariza al batería como estrella; Bunny Berigan, Harry James, Ziggy Elman, Jess Stacy y luego Mel Powell y Eddie Sauter dan a la banda una modernidad propia, la que el bebop no siguió. Las bandas blancas tuvieron ventajas que Henderson nunca tuvo.

scenes.name: Charlie Christian y la guitarra eléctrica
scenes.author: Ted Gioia
scenes.desc: Un chico de Oklahoma City que tocaba en el Ritz Cafe por siete dólares y medio, recomendado por Mary Lou Williams a John Hammond: Goodman lo desdeña («un palurdo increíble») hasta que improvisan una hora sobre «Rose Room». En menos de dos años de grabaciones con el sexteto de Goodman define la guitarra eléctrica en el jazz con líneas de una sola nota, saltos interválicos, tresillos y tensiones cromáticas, frases que los guitarristas copiarán como un canon. Sus noches en el Minton's lo convierten en pionero del bebop; la tuberculosis lo mata en 1942.

scenes.name: Billie Holiday
scenes.author: Ted Gioia
scenes.desc: Con una octava y media de registro y poca potencia, Holiday convierte en canción artística cualquier desecho de Tin Pan Alley gracias a un sentido del compás inigualable, un fraseo relajado y una hondura emocional que es su verdadero virtuosismo. Hammond la descubre en 1933; con Teddy Wilson y, desde 1937, con Lester Young («Pres», que la llama «Lady Day») graba una «historia de amor musical» («All of Me», «Foolin' Myself»). En 1939 «Strange Fruit», sobre un linchamiento, la politiza; se vuelve intérprete de canciones sombrías («Lover Man», «God Bless the Child»), mientras la heroína, la cárcel y la prohibición de cantar en los clubes de Nueva York la hunden. Con Norman Granz rehabilita su carrera con una voz rota pero más madura, y en 1957 canta «Fine and Mellow» por televisión con Lester. Muere en 1959 bajo arresto.

podcast.title: "Primitive Music" Narrative
podcast.body: Hammond was among "progressive white men" who put forward a "deeply mistaken" narrative about "primitive music," characterizing black musical forms as less sophisticated due to their sound in the 1930s. "most of the narrative about primitive music, a narrative that was put forward by very progressive white men like John Hammond or the Lomaxes, is deeply mistaken."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Cafe Society Booking
podcast.body: He booked Sister Rosetta Tharp to play at the Cafe Society, an integrated club, after the Cotton Club closed. "a venue booked by John Hammond, which was an integrated club and which fit her rather better."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 5: "This Train" by Sister Rosetta Tharpe

podcast.title: Disappointment with Aretha's Columbia Years
podcast.body: John Hammond later expressed disappointment with how Columbia Records presented Aretha Franklin's talents to the world, despite signing her himself. He felt the label did not adequately showcase her gifts during her tenure there. "Even John Hammond later said he was disappointed with how the label presented Franklin's gifts to the world."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Say a Little Prayer Edition Part 1

podcast.title: Introducer of Robert Johnson to Dylan
podcast.body: Hammond gave Bob Dylan an unreleased re-issue of old blues records, "King of the Delta Blues Singers" by Robert Johnson, to listen to. He had previously wanted Johnson to perform at "Spirituals to Swing" but learned of his death. "Hammond also gave Dylan an album to take home and listen to, a record which hadn't come out yet, a v-issue of some old blues records called King of the Delta Blues Singers by Robert James."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 97: "Song to Woody" by Bob Dylan

podcast.title: Legendary Talent Scout and Producer
podcast.body: John Hammond was a legendary talent scout, record producer, and label executive, instrumental in shaping the careers of numerous iconic artists. He discovered and signed Aretha Franklin to Columbia Records in 1960. "Thanks largely to the influence of legendary talent scout, record producer, and label executive John Hammond."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
srcs.episode: Say a Little Prayer Edition Part 1

podcast.title: Organiser of Spirituals to Swing
podcast.body: John Hammond was known for his legendary "spirituals to swing" concerts at Carnegie Hall, which were important but also problematic in their narrative of musical evolution. "John Hammond's legendary spirituals to swing concerts."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 5: "This Train" by Sister Rosetta Tharpe

podcast.title: Organizer of Spirituals to Swing Concerts
podcast.body: John Hammond was the organizer of the influential 1938 "Spirituals to Swing" concerts at Carnegie Hall, which later became an album and influenced Bob Dylan. "Hammond had, of course, organised the spirituals to swing concerts which had influenced Dylan"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 97: "Song to Woody" by Bob Dylan

podcast.title: Producer of Dylan's Debut
podcast.body: Hammond produced Bob Dylan's first album, finding Dylan "incredibly difficult to work with" due to his microphone technique and refusal of second takes. "Hammond found Dylan incredibly difficult to work with, saying he had a pulling mic technique"

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 97: "Song to Woody" by Bob Dylan

podcast.title: Producer's Rejection of "Strange Fruit"
podcast.body: John Hammond, Billy Holiday's producer and known for progressive actions like integrating Benny Goodman's band and sponsoring Communist Party shows, found "Strange Fruit" too political and inflammatory to release. "That song was too political, even for her producer, John Hammond."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 4: "Choo Choo Ch'Boogie" by Louis Jordan

podcast.title: Signing Bob Dylan
podcast.body: Hammond was impressed by Bob Dylan, deciding to sign him to Columbia Records despite resistance from Mitch Miller, the head of A&R, who didn't understand Hammond's vision for Dylan. Hammond's strong track record at the label secured the deal. "He decided to sign Dylan, and even though Mitch Miller, Columbia's head of A&R at the time, had no clue what Hammond saw in Dylan."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 97: "Song to Woody" by Bob Dylan

podcast.title: Talent Scout and Producer
podcast.body: A highly influential figure, Hammond discovered artists like Billy Holiday, Count Basie, and Charlie Christian. He later worked for Columbia Records, where he produced Aretha Franklin's first secular records. "he'd been the person to discover Billy Holiday, and Count Basie, and Charlie Christian."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 97: "Song to Woody" by Bob Dylan

podcast.title: Vast Roster of Discoveries
podcast.body: Hammond was known for his staggering roster of discoveries, which included Billy Holiday, Count Basie, and Pete Seeger, and later Bruce Springsteen. He was particularly active in the early 1960s, signing both Detroit native Aretha Franklin and a young Bob Dylan from Duluth, Minnesota, in the same year. "Among Hammond's staggering roster of discoveries were Billy Holiday, Count Basie, Pete Seeger, and later Bruce Springsteen."
